Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
ruminate about how to get even with assailant

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the event I feel intense shame
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
There is something wrong with me as a person
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

vignette: Elena had never meant to walk through the parking garage after midnight. As hotel manager, she had simply forgotten that the evening's housekeeping crew would finish at nine, not eleven. The fluorescent lights hummed overhead, casting long shadows against the concrete pillars. A man emerged from the service corridor, wearing a faded olive windbreaker. He did not ask her for anything. He simply stepped into her path, his hand closing around her wrist before she could turn. The struggle was brief, the weight of him pressing her against a support column, the cold metal of his silver ring biting into her shoulder. She remembered the exact shade of his eyes, the rhythm of his breathing, the way the light caught the band on his third finger. There was no narrative that made sense of it in the moment, only a suffocating certainty that she would not leave alive. In the weeks that followed, Elena tried to explain the incident to Mateo, but the moment the words reached her throat, they fractured. She knew what had happened, yet she could not find the vocabulary to hold it. When she pressed herself to remember, a wave of shame rose in her chest, so sharp she would stop mid-sentence, her face burning. Even to herself, the sequence refused to align. She could not trace a clear line from the garage to the aftermath. Her body, meanwhile, kept operating as if the danger were still active. A heavy set of keys jingling in the lobby would make her shoulders lock. The quiet hum of the security cameras triggered a sudden, breathless rush of panic. She lay awake while her pulse hammered against her ribs, certain that her own nervous system had turned traitor. She had come to believe that something was fundamentally wrong with her as a person. If she had been different, if she had acted differently, it would not have happened. The thought did not arrive as a crisis; it arrived as a fact. She avoided the downtown sector where men in olive jackets congregated, crossing the street or ducking into coffee shops at the first sight of a familiar cut of fabric or the glint of a silver band on a stranger's hand. At the same time, she began staying at the hotel long after closing. Every morning, she walked the same route to the service entrance, scanning the loading docks for familiar silhouettes. When a maintenance supervisor arrived in a green utility vest, she called in sick for three consecutive days. She did not stop the fear; she simply changed the venue. Inside her office, the phone rang with guest inquiries, but she let them go to voicemail. She pulled up the annual budget, then the fire marshal's inspection report, then the staff scheduling spreadsheet. The screen's glow became her only companion. Overwork became a daily ritual. Her hands stayed busy, and her mind stayed elsewhere. In those late, solitary hours behind her desk, her thoughts inevitably turned to him. She mapped out his routine, his name, the exact manner of retribution she wanted. The planning felt like a duty, a way to reclaim the power she had lost. Mateo noticed the distance first. He noticed the missed dinners, the way she flinched when a delivery driver knocked on the hotel doors, the way she could no longer sit through a full conversation without her hands trembling. He stopped asking about the garage. Elena finally called a therapist not because the work had stopped, but because her body no longer listened to her attempts to outrun it. She sat in the intake room, her palms pressed flat against her knees, hoping to finally speak the story without the shame choking her. Most of all, she wanted to stop believing she was the kind of person who deserved what happened to her, and to find a way to live inside her own skin without bracing for a shadow that no longer existed.
